experiment_A_before_after_rollback.methodology: scripts/measure/run.sh -c -p cisc-w2026-seeded /tmp/a.json, run unmodified, on a host seeded fresh by scripts/measure/seed.sh. Phase mapping to the task's S0-S3: before=S0 (seeded, untouched), after=S1 (post `hostveil fix --all --yes`, nothing restarted), restarted=S2 (S1 + `docker compose up -d` on every stack + sysctl --system + sshd reload), reviewed=S3 (S2 + `hostveil fix --all --review --yes` + restart again). check.py's exit code for this run was 0 (both of its promises held: rollback fidelity and score-improved).

ss_vs_external_scan_discrepancy.observation: In the 'restored' phase, `ss -ltn` reports port 6379 (native, non-Docker Redis, from seed.sh's exposed-datastore step) bound to 0.0.0.0, but the off-host container scan does NOT report it reachable. Conversely, ports 5432/6380/8080/8096/9000 (all Docker-published container ports) show as both wildcard-bound AND externally reachable, even though ufw is verified 'active' with a default-deny-incoming policy that allows only port 22.

verified_state_after_restore.ufw_status_verbose: Status: active / Default: deny (incoming), allow (outgoing), deny (routed) / rules: 22/tcp ALLOW IN Anywhere (v4+v6)
verified_state_after_restore.redis_conf_after_rollback: bind 0.0.0.0 / protected-mode no (matches seed.sh's original seeded values -- the file edit rolled back correctly)

ss_vs_external_scan_discrepancy.root_cause: ufw's rules apply to the host's own INPUT chain, which the native redis-server process is filtered by. Docker inserts its own iptables DNAT/FORWARD rules for every `-p host:container` published port, and those take effect ahead of ufw's filter chain -- this is the exact mechanism hostveil's own `firewall.docker-bypass` finding (internal/check/firewall) exists to describe. So after rollback, ufw is genuinely enabled and genuinely blocking the one native service it can see (6379), while every Docker-published port remains reachable regardless of ufw state. ss and the external scan are both telling the truth; they are answering different questions (what is bound vs. what a packet filter actually stops), and this is not a measurement bug.
ss_vs_external_scan_discrepancy.why_ufw_is_still_enabled_after_a_full_ro: `firewall.inactive`'s registered fix is Auto-declared but exec-floored to Review (AGENTS.md: the exec floor in fix.Fix.EffectiveKind) because `ufw enable` is a command, not a file edit, so applyExec keeps no checkpoint. hostveil's own rollback engine has nothing to undo for it -- this is expected residue, not a bug, and is part of why reviewed.not_reversible=16 and residue_expected=true for this run.

experiment_B_rollback_fidelity.methodology: Same run as Experiment A. Paths watched = every absolute path any `hostveil scan --json` finding pointed at (metadata/evidence), plus every file under /etc/sysctl.d, SHA-256'd BEFORE any fix ran (the live filesystem, not hostveil's own checkpoints -- scripts/measure/instruments/rollback.sh candidates+hash). Re-hashed after full rollback (`hostveil rollback <id>` newest-first over every checkpoint created during the run).

paths_not_restored_with_individual_cause.cause: Content-level change, not just permissions. `ssh.emptypasswords`'s local-account half (internal/fix/accounts.go, buildLocalEmptyPasswordFix or equivalent) runs `passwd -l <account>` as an ActionExec against the seeded `contractor` account (empty password from seed.sh's shadow-readable step). ActionExec has no backup -- applyExec records the outcome after running, with nothing file-backed to restore (AGENTS.md: 'Apply order is always backup -> write ... applyExec is the odd one -- commands run first and the record is written after, with no backup at all'). This is deliberate: hostveil cannot and should not restore an empty password. Confirmed real and not a chmod-only artifact: `fileperms.shadow`'s own permission-only fix (0640) for this same file DID roll back exactly -- current mode is 644 (the seeded value), verified directly with `stat` after restore.

hostveil's own edit (accounts.local-banner, an ActionEdit / Auto fix with a checkpoint) rolled back correctly -- the currently-restored file content has NO banner text. The hash mismatch against the pre-fix baseline is caused by an UNRELATED event in the same measurement window: `dpkg.log` on the VM shows `upgrade base-files:amd64 13ubuntu10.4 13ubuntu10.5` at 2026-09-10 05:10:44, which is the package that ships /etc/issue's default content, triggered as a side effect of `apt-get install unattended-upgrades` (the exec half of `updates.disabled`'s review fix pulling in a routine apt index refresh). The rollback-fidelity methodology (a single before/after SHA-256 diff) cannot distinguish 'hostveil failed to restore' from 'hostveil restored correctly, then the OS's own package manager rewrote the file for an unrelated reason' -- both produce the same hash mismatch.
paths_not_restored_with_individual_cause.note: Not a hostveil defect; a limitation of hash-diff-only rollback verification when other processes can also write to a watched path during the measurement window.

paths_not_restored_with_individual_cause.cause: Same root cause and same evidence as /etc/issue above (also owned by base-files).

experiment_B_rollback_fidelity.paths_with_unobserved_before_state_note: These four entries are `/usr/bin/x86_64-linux-gnu-as` and `...-ld.bfd`, which only appear because they were installed fresh by a package (build-essential/binutils, pulled in transitively) after the 'before' hash was taken -- report.py's rollback_verdict only excuses a newly-appeared path from this bucket if it falls under an enumerated directory (/etc/sysctl.d); these do not, so they are flagged even though they are not hostveil findings at all. Recorded as-is, not silently dropped.

experiment_C_control.methodology: A SEPARATE, freshly re-seeded VM (not the same instance as Experiment A/B, and not reused across attempts -- see execution_notes for why a first attempt on this VM had to be discarded and the host re-seeded). `scripts/measure/run.sh -C -c -p cisc-w2026-control /tmp/c.json`, which runs its OWN 'before' measurement, then calls scripts/measure/control.sh internally (CIS Docker Benchmark + Lynis-suggestion-shaped hardening -- sshd, sysctl, file perms, the UID-0 twin account, the Docker daemon config -- with zero reference to hostveil's fix registry), restarts the compose stacks, then measures 'controlled'. hostveil applied nothing in this experiment.

verification_commands: getent passwd breakglass -> exit 2 (no such entry)
id breakglass -> "id: 'breakglass': no such user", exit 1
account_deletion_step_verification.explanation: control.sh runs `userdel -f "$u"` with no `2>/dev/null || true` (control.sh's own comment documents a PAST version of this script that swallowed this exact error and silently deleted nothing). GNU userdel still PRINTS the 'currently used by process 1' warning even with -f, because the UID-0 twin shares PID 1's UID -- but -f forces the deletion through anyway. Confirmed empirically in this run, not assumed from the log message: the account is genuinely gone afterward.

axis_that_got_worse.evidence: listeners_public_tcp delta shows port 9000 (portainer's web UI) newly bound wildcard in the 'controlled' phase, absent in 'before'.
axis_that_got_worse.likely_cause: Timing, not control.sh's action: this VM was re-seeded immediately before the run started, and portainer's container appears to have still been starting when the 'before' instrument sweep ran. control.sh never touches ports, ufw, or compose files, so it cannot itself be responsible for a new port appearing. Reported as an honest, unresolved discrepancy rather than smoothed over -- not independently re-verified with a second run because doing so would require re-seeding this host a third time.

followup_investigation.method: Reproduced the killed-attempt scenario directly on a fresh, separately seeded VM: launched `run.sh -C` via the same vagrant ssh wrapper used in the real run, waited until it reached the exact same log line the two real kills stopped at ('hashing the before-state of every path a finding points at'), then killed the LOCAL wrapper process (TaskStop) the same way the memory watchdog did, and inspected the guest VM afterward.

finding_1_orphaned_remote_process.observation: Killing the local `vagrant ssh -c '...'` process does NOT terminate the remote command on the guest. The remote run.sh (and its child rollback.sh candidates / hostveil scan --json) was reparented to PID 1 and kept running after the local wrapper died.
finding_1_orphaned_remote_process.lifecycle_observed: The orphan survived only briefly: it completed one in-flight `hostveil scan --json` (read-only) and then appears to have exited on its own shortly after -- consistent with the remote bash process receiving SIGPIPE on its next stdout write once the SSH channel closed. It did NOT reach control.sh or any docker command before exiting.
finding_1_orphaned_remote_process.implication: This is a real, previously undocumented gap in the harness/tooling combination (a host-side kill of the SSH wrapper leaves an orphan on the guest), worth disclosing on its own, but in this reproduction it did not survive long enough to mutate container or docker-compose state -- so it does NOT look like a sufficient explanation for the ports-axis discrepancy in the original run.

finding_2_portainer_bind_timing.observation: On a completely fresh reproduction VM, immediately after seed.sh finished, port 9000 was ALREADY listening (docker ps: mgmt-portainer-1 'Up 51 seconds', RestartCount=0, no health check configured). demo/stacks/mgmt/docker-compose.yml publishes 9000:9000 with no healthcheck/depends_on, so the host-side docker-proxy listener binds essentially at container start, not when the app inside finishes initializing.
finding_2_portainer_bind_timing.implication: This weakens the original 'portainer was still starting during the before-phase scan' hypothesis as a generic explanation -- under normal conditions the bind is near-instant, and run.sh -C's own setup (path hashing, then 5 separate before-phase instruments) takes far longer than that before the listeners check actually runs.

followup_investigation.conclusion: Neither candidate mechanism tested here fully explains the original before/controlled divergence for port 9000. Root cause NOT conclusively confirmed: the original VM was already destroyed before this discrepancy was investigated, and container-startup races are inherently non-deterministic, so the exact original conditions could not be replayed. What IS newly confirmed and worth keeping regardless: (1) killing the vagrant-ssh wrapper on the host does not kill the remote command, which is a real fix-it-later item for the harness or for how this session drives it, and (2) portainer's port bind is not, on its own, generally slow enough to explain a several-minute-later divergence, which narrows -- without eliminating -- transient container-start failure (of the kind actually observed independently: mgmt-watchtower-1 in this same reproduction exited immediately with 'client version 1.25 is too old', proving containers in this exact stack CAN fail shortly after start) as the more likely remaining explanation.

execution_notes_and_deviations: Experiment C required a discarded first attempt: control.sh was run manually once (to directly verify the account-deletion step in isolation), which then meant the VM was no longer in a pristine seeded state for run.sh -C's own internal 'before' measurement. The VM was re-seeded from scratch before the reported run.sh -C execution; the manual control.sh run is kept in this report only as supplementary account-deletion evidence, not as part of the before/controlled comparison.

Two attempts at running the Experiment C harness were killed by this session's own background-task memory watchdog due to host memory pressure unrelated to hostveil (the development machine's desktop session -- browser, chat client, game client -- was consuming most of 14GB RAM alongside the 2GB measurement VM). The user freed memory on the host between attempts; the run that is reported here is the one that completed (RUNSH_EXIT=0). This is disclosed because the task instructions require reporting retries rather than silently keeping only a clean-looking run -- the retries here were due to host resource contention, not because earlier attempts produced unfavorable data (no measurement data was produced by the killed attempts; they died during initial path-hashing, before any phase completed).
Experiment A and B share one run (scripts/measure/run.sh's rollback block is exactly Experiment B).
